summary: Back light of the Chapel Hill range pair in Monmouth County, NJ; lit 1856 to guide ships into Chapel Hill Channel, discontinued 1957; now a private house.

structures.note: 40 ft from base to center of lantern; brick foundation; square tower with a light turret (USLHS, LighthouseFriends)
Keepers' house; painted white; addition on east end later (LighthouseFriends)

access.note: Privately owned residence at the end of a long driveway. LighthouseFriends: grounds, dwelling and tower closed; the US Lighthouse Society lists it as not open to the public.

events.note: Government purchases three acres on the hill from Timothy Mount
Tower and keepers' quarters built of wood on brick foundations
Gale blows down the station's outbuildings; rebuilt quickly
Two black screens, about 25 ft by 40 ft, set on either side of the house against winter snow
Chapel Hill Range Cut channel buoys lit electrically through submarine cables from Sandy Hook; the report does not link this to the light
Discontinued as a war measure on 28 April 1898; relighted 1 August 1898
Illuminant changed from mineral oil to incandescent oil vapor on 20 January 1907; intensity increased
Beacon on a steel tower about 200 ft north of the house replaces it
Sold at a General Services Administration auction to a private buyer for $16,313

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The US Lighthouse Society's record gives 222 feet (67.7 m) above mean high water. LighthouseFriends gives a focal plane of 224 feet (68.3 m) above the bay. The record keeps 67.7 m (the USLHS figure). The sources do not explain the two-foot difference.

notes_for_editor: Thin-to-moderate evidence: the USLHS roster and LighthouseFriends carry most facts; the Light-House Board volumes (1892, 1895, 1897, 1899) add the channel, oil house, buoys and the 1898 war darkening. Not in the corpus: the 1853-1857 construction records, the 1907 change, the 1957 deactivation and the 1959 sale; these rest on LighthouseFriends alone and need a primary check (Light-House Board reports for 1856-1858 and 1957, GSA sale records, NJ newspapers 1959). The 1871 gale and the 1874 screens are LighthouseFriends only. Richard Carlow Jr. as builder is LighthouseFriends only; no primary source checked. The Wikipedia lead (not cited) gives a tower of 55 ft originally, 45 ft now, and a 1957 steel tower 200 ft from the old one; LighthouseFriends and USLHS say 40 ft. The 1892 channel passage (scan 634, within the FY1892 report) has an unconfirmed printed page and the page image has not been read; check the page before publication. The OCR reads 'Chanel Hill beacon' on the 1899 page (scan 108); the entry is numbered 367. Keeper names are USLHS spellings; LighthouseFriends variants are noted per line. No wreck or rescue is recorded for this light in any source read. A commercial guide site (shore-guide.com) describes a brownstone tower and 1956 deactivation; not used because it is unsourced and contradicts USLHS (wood) and LighthouseFriends (1957). The 1959 buyer is deliberately not named (a private individual; only his role is given). Lens: LighthouseFriends says the lens formerly used here is the Barbier and Fenestre lens shown at Navesink Lighthouse; its order and whether it is a Fresnel lens are not stated. Fact-check 2026-10-28: all 68 quotes were found on the first run. Checked against the cached USLHS and LighthouseFriends pages and the Light-House Board volumes. Scan pages 259 and 324 (1897 buoys and cables) fall in the fiscal-1897 part of annualreportlig02statgoog, which opens with the fiscal-1896 report; the 1892 passage (scan 634) falls in the fiscal-1892 part of annualreportlig03statgoog, which also holds fiscal 1891. The 1892 printed page is unconfirmed (OCR reads 249?); the story cites the scan page. The USLHS roster starts John Morrison in 1855, a year before the 1856 tower date; the story states the gap and no source explains it. Fixed in the text: the 1899-1910 keeper count, the attribution of the owners and addition, the purpose (not the use) of the observatory, the paraphrase of the winter-visibility and driveway passages, the Navesink footnote and the Carlow wording. The story has six chapters for a moderate evidence base (USLHS, LighthouseFriends, four Board volumes); left for the owner to decide whether to merge.
